title: The hidden therapist: Evidence for a central role of music in psychedelic therapy

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, or with different music. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist. In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked and resonated with the music, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same visit (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same visit, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, the raters agreed only moderately (r 0.6), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say causal inference is problematic without a control condition. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) blamed disagreeable music for their most challenging experience, which was not associated with how challenging they rated it (beta 0.05, p = 0.19), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music blamed by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613.
